The Allied rock-wallaby (Petrogale assimilis) inhabits the rugged, rocky outcrops of northern Queensland, where it displays a suite of life-history traits finely tuned to a seasonally arid environment. Field studies conducted under typical resting body temperatures of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C] have documented a gestation period lasting 31 days [tg = 31 days], a relatively brief interval for a macropodid of its size. Neonates emerge after this short gestation weighing a mere 0.484 grams [Wwb = 0.484 grams], an altricial state typical of marsupials where the tiny newborn must crawl to the teat immediately following parturition. This extreme altriciality imposes a substantial energetic burden on the lactating female, who must support the joey's development through a prolonged period of milk dependency. The remarkable efficiency of this reproductive strategy is underscored by the species' maximum reproductive rate, calculated with reference to the same 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C] thermal regime, which equates to a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] produced only once each year [F_R_i = once each year].

Weaning represents a critical nutritional transition for the young rock-wallaby, marking the endpoint of exclusive maternal provisioning. Long-term observational data indicate that weaning occurs at 296 days after birth [tx = 296 days after birth], a milestone reached when the juvenile first achieves nutritional independence from its mother's milk at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. At this juncture, the offspring's body mass has increased substantially from its neonatal condition, and recorded wet weight at weaning reaches approximately 1700 grams [Wwx = approximately 1700 grams]. This mass stands in stark contrast to the initial birth mass, reflecting the rapid growth trajectory supported by lipid-rich pouch milk during the extended suckling period. The pre-weaning interval imposes heavy metabolic demands on the female, who must allocate considerable resources to lactation while simultaneously maintaining her own body condition in a landscape where forage quality fluctuates markedly with seasonal rainfall patterns across their fragmented habitat.

Puberty in this species is attained relatively late compared to many small-bodied mammals, a pattern consistent with the slow-paced life history of medium-sized macropodids. Under the ambient thermal conditions typical of their active rest phase, recorded at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 525 days [tp = 525 days]. This developmental delay is thought to be ecologically linked to the need for young individuals to acquire sufficient body size and social knowledge of the complex rocky terrain before attempting reproduction. The achievement of sexual maturity does not, however, guarantee immediate breeding; females often defer their first reproductive attempt until they have secured a favorable home range with adequate shelter crevices and food resources. The protracted juvenile period, combined with a low annual reproductive output, renders population growth rates particularly sensitive to increases in sub-adult mortality, a vulnerability exacerbated by introduced predators such as foxes and feral cats in the region.

The species attains a maximum recorded longevity of 4745 days [am = 4745 days], equivalent to approximately 13 years of life under natural conditions, with these estimates again referenced to the 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C] basal temperature baseline used in metabolic comparisons. Such a lifespan is notably extended for a mammal of this body mass, positioning the Allied rock-wallaby among the longer-lived members of the genus Petrogale. Adult body mass plateaus considerably beyond the weaning stage, with the ultimate wet weight of fully grown individuals documented at 4300 grams [Wwi = 4300 grams]. This asymptotic mass is achieved gradually as the skeleton and musculature continue developing through the sub-adult phase. The combination of low fecundity and extended lifespan aligns with predictions from life-history theory for species inhabiting stable but resource-poor environments, where adult survival is prioritized over high reproductive turnover. Predation pressure from wedge-tailed eagles and pythons may further favor the evolution of increased longevity and delayed reproduction.

Comparative analyses within the Petrogale genus reveal that the reproductive schedule of P. assimilis represents a moderate strategy relative to its congeners, neither as accelerated as that of smaller rock-wallabies nor as prolonged as that of the larger species inhabiting temperate zones. The extreme altriciality reflected in the neonatal mass of 0.484 grams [Wwb = 0.484 grams] is a defining marsupial trait, positioning this species among the smaller-bodied members of its genus. The 1700 gram [Wwx = 1700 gram] weaning mass represents approximately 40 percent of the asymptotic adult body mass of 4300 grams [Wwi = 4300 grams], indicating that substantial somatic growth continues after nutritional independence. The generation time, computed from the age at first reproduction combined with a gestation interval of 31 days [tg = 31 days] and an average inter-birth interval of one year, further emphasizes the slow life-history pace of this species at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. Understanding these demographic parameters is crucial for conservation planning, particularly as climate change threatens to alter the timing of resource pulses in the species' already marginal habitat.
